transcription.notes: Two ink lines at the top; the rest is show-through from side 1. Read once by the first agent; line 2 re-read on the image on 14 Nov 2026 (dudout): GANI[Z?][?]ING is GANISING (the Z is part of the I-sign before it; the unread sign is the torn box of S).

system.summary: Symbol substitution of the Jordan-Greenhow cipher: one sign per letter (26 on the 1864 key, plus a second N form), with digraph and code signs on the key sheet; words separated by dots, clear words mixed in.
system.doubled_letters: written twice (ATTACK, WILL, EFFORT, FERRY, ALARM on side 1); the key sheet's rule 'second letter inverted' not seen
system.sibling_key: 1864 Greenhow key (NARA M1091 naId 62017285 image 0484, 'Lamb Papers CXXIX'); used. The same key reads Jordan's 1861 letter (targets/jordan1861).
system.notes: distinct_symbols = distinct sign labels on side 1. The key sheet's digraph and code signs were not identified on side 1.

prior_solution.where: None found: the NARA record has no scope note or decipherment; the Library of Congress / World Digital Library copy (wdl.2706) and the Santa Clara University exhibit (item 3281) show the letter without a transcription; phrase searches found nothing. The Official Records Ser. II vol. 2 (Greenhow case papers, pp. 561-577), Pinkerton's Spy of the Rebellion (1883) and Greenhow's My Imprisonment (1863) do not print it (text searches, 27 Oct 2026). Fishel, The Secret War for the Union (1996) and Blackman, Wild Rose (2005) were checked by web search only (lending-library copies, full text not reachable). A period Union decipherment cannot be excluded: OR II 2 p. 561 says fragments were 'placed together so as to be read and copied'.

conditions.human_role: Outside contribution (WAINUT): the operator chose the catalogue item; transcription, key reading, decode, controls and prior-art search were done by AI language-model agents and checked against the images. No hand correction of readings recorded.
tools: decode.py (key applied to shape labels; controls against the English word list in lang/lexicons)

solution.what: Fetched the four images of NARA naId 1634036 and images 0482-0486 of M1091 naId 62017285.
Read the symbol column of M1091 image 0484 (the 1864 key found on Greenhow's body); image 0483 is a different table. Header 'Lamb Papers CXXIX'.
Transcribed side 1 twice: by key value, and independently in neutral shape labels (transcription_side1.txt). Side 2 (two lines) and the numeral fragment (image 3) transcribed once.

Applied the key to side 1: attack is hourly expected, they believe the attack will be simultaneous, an effort is being made to find out who gave the alarm, a troop of cavalry, Harper's Ferry. A second N form, not on the key sheet, valued from context. Restorations at paper losses marked.

decode.py: true key 17/27 whole cipher words in the English word list, mean bigram -2.49; 2,000 random keys mean 0.5, max 5, bigram z = 5.6; key shifted +1: 4/27; signs shuffled inside words: mean 2.6, max 6.
Side 2: two ink lines give only fragments (gr..e, tim.., bo.., ..ganiz.ing). Not read.

NARA record, LoC/WDL wdl.2706, Santa Clara University exhibit item 3281, phrase searches: no decipherment found. NARA naId 1634043, a clear pencil draft headed 10 Aug 1861 on McClellan's activity and an expected attack, is close in theme; it is not a copy of this letter.

Review (Claude, for Daniel Bourdeau), print step: grepped the archive.org texts of the Official Records Ser. II vol. 2 (warofrebellion02unit_0; the Greenhow case papers, pp. 561-577), Pinkerton's Spy of the Rebellion (1883; Gutenberg 34973) and Greenhow's My Imprisonment (1863) for the side-1 phrases ('hourly expected', 'gave the alarm', 'panic', 'simultaneous', 'Harper's Ferry', 'cavalry') and for 'mourning'. None prints this letter or a decipherment of it. OR II 2 p. 561 says her cipher letters were found torn in the stove and some fragments 'assorted and placed together so as to be read and copied'; pp. 564-565 print Jordan's letter of 29 Oct 1861 (cipher arranged 'last April', alias Thomas John Rayford); Greenhow (1863, pp. 76-77) says the agents puzzled over her cipher scraps for seven days. Fishel (1996) and Blackman (2005) are lending-library copies on archive.org whose full text could not be searched; web searches for the phrases with either book found nothing. Six web searches in all.

Review: tested the numeral scrap (image 3) against the 1864 key sheet. The key's figure row writes 1-9 as letter-like signs (a, d, phi, ff, m, b, nn, c, c; 10 = III), so Arabic figures are not this key's numbers. Read as the key's digit-like letter signs (3 C, 4 I/R, 5 O, 7 B, 8 G, 9 K, 0 J, $ U), 11 of the 33 figure groups contain a 2 or 6, which has no letter value, and no group gives a word; the scrap's clear letters are not figure signs either (numerals_test.py). The figures (5 ... 104, with '$5 dollers $25') read as a money reckoning. The last line has three key-like signs (box with X = S, box with dot = M, Y = E) among torn clear letters: too short to read.

Review (Claude, for Daniel Bourdeau): side 1 reading re-read against decryption_side1.txt and image 1 (lines 4-9 checked sign by sign: ATTACK IS HOURLY EXPEC-R-TED, THEY BELEIVE, SIMULTANEOU, FERR-). Grade B: coherent, but holes or conjectures in 9 of 15 sentences. Side 2 counted from transcription_side2.txt (17 signs read; no clear words), filling the two 'unknown' fields.

Brice Dudout (Claude Opus 5.5): an independent script (verify_dudout_20261114.py) applies the label legend of transcription_side1.txt to the 183 signs of side 1: 17 of 17 lines as in decryption_side1.txt. Side 1 and side 2 checked on the NARA images (naId 1634036, images 1-2), the key on M1091 image 0484. Side 2, line 2, read once before, is GANISING, '[or]ganising': the '[Z?]' is the two extra strokes of the I-sign (as the I of MORNING on side 1) and the unread sign is the lower half of the box with X (S). The G of MORNING is a closed 8 with a stroke, so the stroke alone does not tell G from U (the U of OUT is the key's open $).

Project check of PR #572 (Brice Dudout): his side-1 script re-run (24 labels, 183 signs, 17 of 17 lines equal decryption_side1.txt). Side 2 line 2 (GANISING) taken on his record: the NARA catalogue returned no image link to a script this session, so the re-read was not repeated here. Read share of side 1 recounted with v10_relabel.share: 30 words, 31 holes, 0.492; read_share and fraction_read set to it in place of 0.595 (v2_score's hole rate, a different count); README, SOLVED_CATALOGUE, SOLVED_RANKING, findings and manifest lines brought into line. Class unchanged (read in part). Page: side-2 fragment line corrected.

outcome.method: read after matching with key from external sources
outcome.method_basis: The 1864 key found on Greenhow's body (NARA M1091 naId 62017285 image 0484), not previously tied to this 1861 letter, decodes side 1 with no change except one extra N form; side 2 and the numeral fragment are not read.
outcome.fraction_read_source: reading_side1.md, reading body, counted with research/reading_audit/v10_relabel.py (share): 30 whole words, 31 holes, with every supplied letter and conjecture counted as a hole (0.492 read as sense; recounted 14 Nov 2026; the 0.595 recorded before was the hole rate of v2_score.py, 0.405 over 42 word tokens, a different count); side 2 not counted.
outcome.notes: Applying the 1864 key to 1861 Greenhow material is not new (the Rosenbach did so in 2011 for another note); no decipherment of this letter was found. The second N form (looped l with a crossbar) is not on the key sheet; every word that contains it is otherwise keyed.

tested against the 1864 key (numerals_test.py): its figure signs are letter-like (1 a, 2 d ...), so the Arabic figures are not this key's numbers, and read as its letter signs the figures give no words (2 and 6 have no value); the scrap reads as a money reckoning ('$5 dollers $25'), and the three key-like signs on its last line are too few to read. No other key or code book is known

texts.label: Greenhow, mourning-paper letter, side 1 (naId 1634036 image 1)

reading_review.note: Read reading_side1.md against decryption_side1.txt and image 1 (lines 4-9 sign by sign). The sentences cohere in her spelling (attack is hourly expected; they believe the attack will be simultaneous; an effort is being made to find out who gave the alarm), and every restoration is marked; but 9 of 15 sentences carry losses or conjectures ('Edwards Ferry', 'Baltimore', 'troop of', 'Harper's Ferry'), so grade B, not A. Replaces the contributor's own grade A (WAINUT agent).

texts.summary: From Washington in summer 1861: McClellan is busy and the panic is great; an attack is hourly expected and they believe it will be simultaneous from [...]rds Ferry (Edwards Ferry?) and [...]timore (Baltimore?); an effort is being made to find out who gave the alarm; a troop of cavalry [...]nt from here this morning; Harper's Ferry is named. Intelligence from the Greenhow ring before her arrest on 23 Aug 1861.
